title: Estimating environmental footprint of bottom-towed fishing gears on the seabed
content:
Abstract
Bottom-towed fishing gears (hereafter fishing gear) disturb the seabed and thereby affect the marine environment. The degree of disturbance depends on the type of fishing gear, fishing intensity, and the composition of the seabed. The Greater North Sea region, which covers the northern European continental shelf, is among the most intensively fished areas globally. Otter trawl, beam trawl, and Danish seine are the most dominant methods used in the region, and their seabed disturbance was therefore examined in this study, focusing on the Danish coast (1500 km2) in the Skagerrak area. Seabed disturbances were assessed using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and sonograms obtained from a towed side-scan sonar (sonar). Three months of fishing events in 2023 were analysed using AIS data, and the sonar covered 19.8 km² of the seabed at depths between 3 and 34 m in sandy sediment. Tracks from fishing gears appeared as visible depressions in the seabed on the sonograms and were identified as originating from beam trawl (335), otter trawl doors (41), and otter trawl ground gear (9); additionally, 5 tracks originated from unspecified ground gear. No tracks were observed from otter trawl sweeps and bridles or from Danish seines. We estimate that tracks from beam trawls remain visible for a maximum of 30 days, while tracks from otter trawls remain visible for a maximum of 7 days. The hourly surface footprint was highest for Danish seine (1.43 km2 h−1) and lowest for beam trawl (0.24 km2 h−1). However, the hourly subsurface footprint was highest for beam trawl (0.24 km2 h−1), up to 20 times higher than for otter trawl (0.01 km2 h−1). The Danish seine had no subsurface footprint, as no tracks were observed. Our results demonstrate that environmental footprints on the seabed vary with the type of bottom-towed fishing gear used and between the seabed surface and subsurface layers. These findings provide quantitative estimates of the surface and subsurface environmental footprints of bottom-towed fishing gears, which can support ecosystem-based fisheries management and spatial planning, that aim to reduce the environmental impacts of fishing gears on the seabed and promote sustainable fishing practices.
